The ancestral transmission kernel models how genetic variance decays exponentially with each generation, expressed as 1/3^n, where n is the number of generations back. This kernel underpins the midparent parity relation, which asserts that the expected trait value of a midparent is one-third that of the offspring, assuming symmetric inheritance. These relations form a dual structure: one describing variance propagation forward in time, the other backward from offspring to ancestors. The trait segregation scaling highlights that stature and eye-colour, while both hereditary, differ in their transmission dynamics, implying distinct genetic architectures. Failure modes include assumption violations such as non-independent traits or non-linear inheritance, which would invalidate the linear scaling laws.
